entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Notre-Dame Cathedral of Paris (Notre-Dame de Paris) is the supreme example of French Gothic architecture, built between 1163 and 1345 CE on the Île de la Cité, heart of medieval Paris, and one of the world's most visited sacred monuments before its devastating 2019 fire. Notre-Dame has witnessed France's most significant historical events for 800 years: Henry VI of England crowned King of France within its walls (1431), Napoleon's coronation as Emperor (1804), Charles de Gaulle's liberation mass (1944), and the funerals of French presidents and military heroes.

Bishop Maurice de Sully began construction in 1163 under Louis VII. Notre-Dame was an architectural laboratory for Gothic innovations: flying buttresses (enabling walls of stained glass), ribbed vaulting, and pointed arches reaching 35 metres. The cathedral's three rose windows — especially the north rose window (1250 CE) — are among the greatest achievements of medieval stained glass art, their deep blues and reds created through techniques partially lost in the 12th century.

The April 2019 fire, broadcast live to the world, destroyed the 19th-century spire and most of the lead roof, and shocked the global public with what felt like the destruction of civilization itself. Emmanuel Macron's promise to rebuild Notre-Dame within five years became a national and global project: €840 million was raised within 48 hours from the Pinault and Arnault families alone. The cathedral is scheduled to reopen in December 2024 — testimony to the power of architectural heritage to mobilize collective resources.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Notre-Dame de Paris — whose 2019 fire mobilized €840 million in 48 hours from across the world — is the building that most dramatically demonstrated that architectural heritage transcends religion, nationality, and politics in its claim on human emotion.
